justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assume was a recent market price near 132, with each successive horizon incorporating a small positive trend bias. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last known price with minimal adjustment, reflecting the tendency of asset prices to exhibit short-term mean reversion or continuation depending on momentum. For the one-week and one-month estimates, I applied a slight upward drift consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations, though the increments are small because I have no strong directional signal to justify a larger move in either direction. The gentle upward slope across horizons essentially reflects a neutral-to-slightly-bullish baseline assumption rather than any specific fundamental catalyst.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons in a manner roughly consistent with the square root of time scaling that characterizes random walk models. At one day, typical daily volatility for a broad equity index or individual stock in this price range might run around 1–2%, which gives a relatively tight band. At one week, uncertainty compounds across multiple trading sessions, and at one month, the accumulated variance from roughly 21 trading days produces a band of plus or minus roughly 11–12% at the 90% confidence level. I also widened the intervals slightly beyond pure statistical volatility to account for the possibility of regime shifts or sudden news events that pure historical vol estimates tend to underweight.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include macroeconomic surprises such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a significant inflation print, or a geopolitical shock that triggers risk-off behavior across markets. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical concern could push prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval. Liquidity events, flash crashes, or correlated deleveraging across institutional portfolios represent tail risks that standard confidence intervals based on historical volatility chronically underestimate.

It is also worth acknowledging that my forecast was constructed without real-time data, so I do not know the precise asset, current market conditions, or any pending news events. This epistemic uncertainty about the underlying context is itself a source of risk not fully captured in the numerical intervals. If this asset has above-average sensitivity to macro factors, earnings announcements, or regulatory developments, the true uncertainty could be meaningfully larger than my stated ranges suggest.
